title: Raise the foundation codec's 512-item ceiling for byte-typed arrays
description:
Filed by governor-7610ed5a (standing authority) from worker-f144c751's measured report (msg-b7275c46, 04:02Z) — do not re-derive.

THE BOUND: `MAX_ITEMS = 512` at apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-attempt-codec.ts:13 bounds `binding.exactBytes`, so the foundation context-manifest codec (task-3e891741's deliverable) refuses any context manifest over 512 rendered bytes — measured: 513 bytes → FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_MALFORMED. Real agent contexts are thousands of bytes.

WHY FILED: the bound is INVISIBLE to every gate — the codec suite is green (fixtures render ~70 bytes), daemon suite 130 files / 2799 tests green. Nothing reds until task-22fa35a5 (ledger writer) feeds a realistic manifest, at which point it presents as a defect in the ledger writer rather than an inherited bound in a shared helper. Same shape as the unrostered-boundary class: a real constraint no gate reports, landing on whoever touches it next.

SCOPE (worker's suggestion, architect decides): own foundation-attempt-codec.ts; either raise MAX_ITEMS for byte-typed arrays specifically or give the shared snapshot helper a bytes-aware path. The DoD must include a test sealing a manifest at REALISTIC size (thousands of bytes) through the real codec. CAUTION: the helper is SHARED with the attempt codec — the attempt-codec suite must stay green under the change, and the bound exists as a hostile-input defense, so the widened path must remain bounded (a larger explicit cap or per-type cap, not unbounded).

SEQUENCING: task-22fa35a5 (Commit the Foundation context manifest before launch) hard-hits this first — its planner should treat this task as a dependency or absorb it with an explicit scope note.
definitionOfDone: A context manifest of realistic size (≥4KB rendered bytes) seals and re-admits through the production codec round-trip with digest match
byte-typed array bounds remain explicit and finite — the hostile oversized-input case still refuses with its exact code
The shared attempt-codec suite and the context-manifest codec suite are both green under the change, run as separate legs with printed nonzero counts
A mutation drill removing the new bound (or restoring the old 512 cap) reddens a NAMED test each way

implementationPlan.description: Reproduce the bound and size the fix from the design's own limits, before choosing a number. THE BOUND: `apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-attempt-codec.ts:13` declares `MAX_DEPTH = 12, MAX_KEYS = 64, MAX_ITEMS = 512` and line 30 enforces `if (keys.length > (array ? MAX_ITEMS : MAX_KEYS)) return HOSTILE` inside `copyValue` — ONE enforcement point, which is what makes this fixable in one place. Write a RED test sealing a context manifest whose `binding.exactBytes` exceeds 512 entries through the REAL context codec and confirm it refuses with `FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_MALFORMED` (worker-f144c751 measured 513 bytes as the first failure). NOW SIZE IT PROPERLY, because 4KB is the DoD floor and not the real requirement: `@moe/context` declares `MAX_JOURNAL_ENTRY_COUNT = 8` and `MAX_JOURNAL_TEXT_CHARACTERS = 12 * 1024` (context-contract.ts:6-7), so journal content ALONE can render ~98,304 characters before mandatory items, optional selection and exclusions are added. A cap chosen to clear 4KB would still refuse a legitimate context. Record that arithmetic in the test file as the justification for the number chosen.
implementationPlan.note:
BOUND REPRODUCED THROUGH PRODUCTION, AND SIZED FROM THE DESIGN'S OWN LIMITS.

THE ENFORCEMENT POINT, confirmed on current bytes: apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-attempt-codec.ts:13 `const MAX_DEPTH = 12, MAX_KEYS = 64, MAX_ITEMS = 512;` and :31 `if (keys.length > (array ? MAX_ITEMS : MAX_KEYS)) return HOSTILE;` inside copyValue — the ONE place the array bound is applied. The path in: foundation-context-manifest-codec.ts admitManifest -> snapshotFoundationValue(value) -> copyValue, and a HOSTILE result becomes `refuse("FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_MALFORMED")`.

REPRODUCTION, run through the REAL @moe/context chain and the REAL codec (node ESM probe, no test helpers):
  rendered exactBytes length: 4158
  ok: false  code: FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_MALFORMED  layer: FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_CODEC
So the refusal is exactly the filed one, at the exact layer. Also measured: a 500-character mandatory item already renders 562 bytes, so the ceiling is crossed by contexts far smaller than anything real — the 512 limit is ~500 characters of content, not 512 characters.

RED TEST LANDED (TDD): "a context of realistic size > seals and re-admits a 4KiB rendered context with a matching digest" fails now, `Test Files 1 failed (1)`, `Tests 1 failed | 54 passed (55)` on the focused run `npx vitest run --root . --config package.json src/work/foundation-context-manifest-codec.test.ts` from apps/daemon. It builds the manifest through selectContext -> renderContext (never hand-forged), seals through encodeFoundationContextManifestRecord and re-admits through decodeFoundationContextManifestRecord, asserting BOTH digests survive. I deliberately did NOT commit a permanent test asserting "513 bytes refuses", because that is the behaviour being removed — it would contradict step 3 and have to be deleted an hour later. The refusal is recorded as evidence above instead.

THE SIZING ARITHMETIC, written into the test file as a header comment so the number is auditable rather than magic. @moe/context publishes DEFAULT_CONTEXT_BYTE_BUDGET = 64 * 1024 = 65,536 rendered bytes, MAX_JOURNAL_ENTRY_COUNT = 8 and MAX_JOURNAL_TEXT_CHARACTERS = 12 * 1024, so journal content ALONE reaches 8 * 12,288 = 98,304 characters before mandatory items, optional selection and exclusions. The test asserts that 98,304 figure from the imported constants, so the justification cannot drift from the package it is derived from. A cap sized to the DoD's 4KiB floor would still refuse a legitimate 64KiB context — which is how this defect was filed.

CHOSEN CEILING (plan's shape, and it clears the arithmetic): reuse this file's own MAX_BYTES = 1_048_576, already enforced on Uint8Array.byteLength at :91 and re-checked on decode, so a byte payload is bounded identically whether it arrives as a typed array or as a JSON number array. 1 MiB > 98,304, so a maximal journal-bearing context fits with room, and nothing becomes unbounded.

ONE DIVERGENCE TO FLAG rather than silently resolve: comment-e91831f4 (architect-f956ffe1, 04:23Z) proposed a different shape — an exact-path 64KiB allowance wired only into the two context-codec snapshot calls, owning four files. The APPROVED PLAN (09:55Z, later) instead puts a per-type byte-aware cap in copyValue reusing MAX_BYTES, owning two files. I am following the approved plan: it is newer, it is what was approved, and 64KiB would sit BELOW the 98,304-character journal arithmetic the same architect's plan recorded. Noted here so QA sees the divergence was measured, not missed.

Peer traffic in the same package (not mine, not touched): apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-context-manifest-ledger.ts + .test.ts are dirty and foundation-context-manifest-identity.ts is untracked. My two owned paths are clean.

implementationPlan.description: Implement a PER-TYPE cap, not a global raise, and get the guard ORDER right — this is the one subtle part. Raising `MAX_ITEMS` itself is rejected: `foundation-attempt-codec.ts` is imported by the evidence service and store, the goal qualification reads, the journal append and reader, and the attempt-release path, so a global raise weakens the hostile-input defence for every one of them. Instead give the array branch a bytes-aware cap: generic arrays keep 512, while an array whose every element is a byte-valued integer gets a larger explicit ceiling. Use the bound this file ALREADY declares for byte content — `MAX_BYTES = 1_048_576`, enforced on `Uint8Array.byteLength` at line 89 — so a byte-typed number array and a Uint8Array carrying the same payload are bounded alike rather than by two unrelated numbers. THE ORDER MATTERS AND IS THE WHOLE DEFENCE: check the HARD ceiling first (`keys.length > MAX_BYTE_ITEMS` -> HOSTILE), and only then, if the length exceeds `MAX_ITEMS`, scan to confirm every element really is a byte. Scanning before the ceiling check would let a hostile ten-million-element array force a full traversal — exactly the denial the cap exists to prevent. The widened path stays explicit and finite, as the filing requires; nothing becomes unbounded.
implementationPlan.note:
PER-TYPE CAP LANDED IN copyValue. Generic arrays still stop at MAX_ITEMS = 512; only an array whose EVERY element is a byte may run to MAX_BYTE_ITEMS, and MAX_BYTE_ITEMS is `MAX_BYTES` itself (1_048_576) rather than a new number — so the same payload is bounded identically whether it arrives as a Uint8Array (byteLength, :91) or as a JSON number array. Two independent byte ceilings would drift and the looser one would become the real bound.

GUARD ORDER, which is the whole defence: the length check answers FIRST, before any traversal (`keys.length > (array ? MAX_BYTE_ITEMS : MAX_KEYS)` -> HOSTILE). A ten-million-element hostile array is refused on its length alone and never walked.

ONE DELIBERATE IMPROVEMENT ON THE PLAN'S SHAPE, flagged because it changes what drill (iii) can target. The plan described a separate pre-scan ("then scan to confirm every element really is a byte"). I folded the byte test into the copy loop that was already going to visit every element: `const bytesOnly = array && keys.length > MAX_ITEMS;` and, inside the existing descriptor loop, `if (bytesOnly && !isByte(descriptor.value)) return HOSTILE;`. Same ordering property (hard ceiling before any per-element work), same per-element strictness, but ONE traversal instead of two, and the check reads the value through the SAME `getOwnPropertyDescriptor` the copy already uses — a separate scan indexing `value[i]` would have invoked accessor properties that the descriptor path deliberately refuses. Consequence for step 6: there is no separate scan to invert, so drill (iii) becomes "move the length check below the loop" instead.

isByte is exact, not approximate: `typeof value === "number" && Number.isInteger(value) && value >= 0 && value <= 255 && !Object.is(value, -0)`. Negative zero is excluded on purpose — `-0 === 0` and `Number.isInteger(-0)` are both true and `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`, so a smuggled -0 would be admitted as one value and re-read as a different one after a canonical round trip. `Object.is` is the only check that sees it.

NOT DONE, on purpose: `MAX_ITEMS` itself is untouched. `grep -rln foundation-attempt-codec apps/daemon/src` reaches the evidence verification service and store, goals/goal-qualification-reads.ts, journal/journal-append.ts, journal/journal-reader.ts and the attempt-release path; a global raise would relax the hostile-input bound for all of them to serve one caller.

EVIDENCE:
- The step-1 red is now green: `npx vitest run --root . --config package.json src/work/foundation-context-manifest-codec.test.ts` -> EXIT 0, `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 55 passed (55)` (was 1 failed | 54 passed).
- The shared helper's four direct consumer suites are green together: foundation-attempt-service.test.ts, evidence/foundation-verification-service.test.ts, goals/goal-qualification.test.ts, work/attempt-release-disposition.test.ts -> EXIT 0, `Test Files 4 passed (4)`, `Tests 106 passed (106)`.
- foundation-attempt-codec.ts is 232 lines, inside the 250 target and well under the 400 split threshold.

FINDING for step 4/5, and a scope note: there is NO apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-attempt-codec.test.ts — the shared codec has no suite of its own today; it is covered only indirectly through those four consumers (`grep -rln foundation-attempt-codec --include=*.test.ts`). DoD 3 names "the shared attempt-codec suite" as a separate leg with a printed count, and comment-e91831f4 listed that file as a deliverable, so I will create it in step 4 with the per-type arms asserted directly against the shared helper (a generic 513-item array still refusing is a property of THIS helper, not of the context codec). That is one path beyond the plan's affectedFiles list, declared here rather than appearing silently in the diff.

implementationPlan.description: Prove the realistic round-trip, DoD 1. Seal a context manifest of at least 4KB of rendered bytes — and, given the arithmetic from step 1, add a second case at a genuinely realistic size (tens of KB) so the cap is proven against the design's real limits rather than against the DoD's floor. Both must pass the PRODUCTION codec round-trip with a matching digest: encode, decode, and assert the recomputed digest equals the sealed one, so the change is shown not to have perturbed canonical bytes at size. Build the manifest through the real `selectContext` -> `renderContext` chain where practical rather than hand-forging a byte array — a hand-built array proves the cap moved but not that a genuine rendered context now survives, which is the actual claim.
implementationPlan.note:
DoD 1 PROVEN AT THREE SIZES, all built through the REAL selectContext -> renderContext chain and sealed through the PRODUCTION codec — no hand-forged byte arrays, so what is proven is that a genuine rendered context survives, not merely that a number moved.

Named cases, from a verbose run (times show real work, not a memoized fixture):
  "seals and re-admits the DoD floor, 4KiB with both digests intact"                     13ms
  "seals and re-admits a realistic full-budget context, 64KiB with both digests intact"  145ms
  "seals and re-admits the design's journal ceiling, 96KiB with both digests intact"     178ms
The second and third sizes are read from @moe/context's own exported constants (DEFAULT_CONTEXT_BYTE_BUDGET and MAX_JOURNAL_ENTRY_COUNT * MAX_JOURNAL_TEXT_CHARACTERS), not typed as literals, so the fixture cannot drift from the package whose limits justify the cap.

Each case asserts four things, and the first two are what keep it from being vacuous:
1. the fixture really is that large — `exactBytes.length > contentBytes` — so a selection that silently dropped content cannot leave the arm proving the small case three times;
2. the seal is ADMITTED (encode ok), which is the behaviour that was refused before the fix;
3. BOTH digests survive the round trip: `decoded.record.recordDigest` equals the sealed outer digest and `decoded.record.manifest.digest` equals the inner one — so widening the bound is shown not to have perturbed canonical bytes at size;
4. `decoded.record.manifest.binding.exactBytes` deep-equals the original array — a truncation that still digested consistently would pass (3) and fail here.

The sizing arithmetic assertion from step 1 stays as its own arm ("renders more bytes than the design's own journal ceiling would need"), pinning 8 * 12,288 = 98,304 against the imported constants.

FOCUSED SUITE: `npx vitest run --root . --config package.json src/work/foundation-context-manifest-codec.test.ts` from apps/daemon -> EXIT 0, `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 57 passed (57)`, up from 55 before this step (the single 4KiB case became a three-case it.each). Duration 3.65s with tests 500ms — the 96KiB case walks ~98k array elements through copyValue and canonical encoding and still lands in 178ms, so the widened path is not pathological.

implementationPlan.description: Prove the defence still holds, DoD 2. The hostile oversized-input case must STILL refuse with its exact code: assert that an array one element past the new byte ceiling is HOSTILE, and that a NON-byte array past 512 is still HOSTILE — the second is what proves the widening is per-type rather than global. Add the adversarial arms the per-type check invites: an array of mostly-bytes with one out-of-range element (513+ entries) must refuse rather than being admitted by a sloppy sample-based check; an array containing a non-integer or a negative value must refuse; and an array containing NEGATIVE ZERO deserves its own arm, since `Object.is(x, -0)` is the only way to see it — `x === 0` and `Number.isInteger(-0)` both pass, and `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`, so it survives a canonical round-trip silently. Each arm asserts the exact refusal code, not merely that something was refused.
implementationPlan.note:
DoD 2 PROVEN — 17 arms in a NEW suite, apps/daemon/src/work/foundation-attempt-codec.test.ts, EXIT 0, `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 17 passed (17)`. Every arm asserts the exact code FOUNDATION_ATTEMPT_REQUEST_MALFORMED through decodeFoundationAttemptRequest, the production surface that maps this helper's sentinel onto a stable code.

WHY THE ARMS ARE HERE AND NOT IN THE CONTEXT SUITE, which the plan's affectedFiles assumed. The context codec validates `exactBytes` ITSELF before the snapshot runs: foundation-context-manifest-codec.ts:161-163 requires `bytes.every((byte) => boundedInteger(byte, 255))`, and boundedInteger at :120-123 already rejects non-integers, negatives, out-of-range values AND `-0` via Object.is. So every per-element arm written against the context codec would be answered by that earlier guard and stay green with my new check deleted — a refusal test answered by the wrong layer. The generic-array half is unreachable through that codec at all. The shared helper's own surface is the only place the per-type rule is observable.

THE PER-TYPE PROOF (this is the arm that fails if MAX_ITEMS had been raised globally):
  "refuses a generic array one item past the limit with the exact code" — 513 strings, refused.
  "admits a generic array exactly at the limit" — 512 strings, admitted, so the arm above is a boundary and not a blanket refusal.
  "refuses an over-length array of mixed values even when most are bytes".

THE CEILING, explicit and finite:
  "admits a byte array at exactly the ceiling" (1,048,576 elements, 146ms — real work, walked not short-circuited)
  "refuses a byte array one element past the ceiling" (38ms — refused on LENGTH before any traversal, which is the guard-order property showing up as a timing difference)
  "is the codec's own request-byte bound, and it is 1 MiB" — pins FOUNDATION_ATTEMPT_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES against a hand-transcribed 1_048_576, so a silent change to the constant reddens instead of being followed.

EVERY ELEMENT MUST EARN IT — seven it.each arms, each with the bad value at the LAST index, the position a sampled or first-element check never looks at: 256, -1, 1.5, "7", null, [7], and NEGATIVE ZERO. Plus the control that keeps them honest: "still admits those same values BELOW the generic limit" — without it, all seven would also pass under a codec that simply refused any array containing a string or a null, and the arms would be testing the wrong rule.

TWO DEPTH ARMS I ADDED after the first attempt failed and taught me the arithmetic: the request object is depth 0, graphSnapshot is visited at depth 1, each wrapper adds one, the array one more, its elements one beyond. Nine wrappers puts the elements at exactly MAX_DEPTH = 12 (admitted); ten refuses. The refusal companion matters — "admits at depth" alone is satisfied by a codec with no depth bound at all.

SCOPE ADDITION, declared: this file is new and was not in the plan's affectedFiles. It is the file comment-e91831f4 named as a deliverable and the one DoD 3 calls "the shared attempt-codec suite" — which did not exist; the helper was covered only through four consumer suites. Owned paths for this task are now three: foundation-attempt-codec.ts, foundation-attempt-codec.test.ts, foundation-context-manifest-codec.test.ts.

NOT DONE, and why rather than silently: no context-level over-ceiling arm. A manifest whose exactBytes exceeds 1 MiB cannot be sealed anyway — deriveFoundationContextRecordDigest canonically encodes the record, exceeds MAX_BYTES, returns "", and the empty digest fails boundedText with the SAME FOUNDATION_CONTEXT_MALFORMED code. The arm would pass without discriminating which guard answered, so it would be evidence of nothing. The ceiling is pinned unambiguously on the helper's own surface instead.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
A PER-TYPE CAP, NOT A GLOBAL RAISE. `MAX_ITEMS = 512` lives in `foundation-attempt-codec.ts`, whose helpers are imported by the evidence verification service and store, the goal qualification reads, the journal append and reader, the attempt-release path and several test harnesses. Raising the constant globally would relax the hostile-input array bound for every one of them to buy one caller a larger context — the filing itself warns the bound "exists as a hostile-input defense" and that the widened path "must remain bounded (a larger explicit cap or per-type cap, not unbounded)". So generic arrays keep 512 and only byte-valued arrays get the larger ceiling.

THE CEILING IS THE FILE'S OWN `MAX_BYTES = 1_048_576`, not a fresh number. That constant already bounds `Uint8Array.byteLength` at line 89, so reusing it means a byte payload is bounded identically whether it arrives as a typed array or as a JSON number array. Inventing a third magic number would leave two byte bounds that can drift apart.

SIZING FROM THE DESIGN, NOT FROM THE DoD FLOOR. DoD 1 says "≥4KB". That is a floor, not the requirement: `@moe/context` allows 8 journal entries of 12,288 characters each, so journal content alone can render ~98KB before anything else is added. A cap chosen to just clear 4KB would still refuse legitimate contexts and the task would be re-filed. The plan records that arithmetic as the justification for the number.

GUARD ORDER IS A DESIGN DECISION, not an implementation detail. A bytes-aware cap needs to know whether every element is a byte, and that scan is itself unbounded work. Checking the hard ceiling FIRST keeps the worst case bounded; scanning first reintroduces exactly the denial-of-service the cap prevents. Called out explicitly because it is invisible in review and no correctness test will catch it.
